metadata.title: ECIS — Episode 17: The Company You Keep

beats.narration_text: Sixteen episodes of reading one company at a time. This one stops pretending a company is the only thing in the room. I'm Anjana.

show.event: ClaudeComposerAsk: greeting 'Hello, Anjana'; ask types itself

props.command: ECIS scores each company on its own transcript, on its own terms. But a signal means something different depending on who that company is connected to, on what the words mean in this industry rather than in general English, and on whether the claim behind it was backed by anything at all. Can it learn to read a company in context?
output: a company becomes a node with neighbours
a mention becomes a pointer into the graph
and a claim gets weighed against its evidence

beats.narration_text: ECIS extracts guidance signals from earnings calls using four readers weighted by a five-dimension triangulator. Tree, sequence, and Temporal Fusion Transformer models forecast revisions across multiple horizons, with regime detection, uncertainty quantification, and selective abstention filtering the output. Analyst intelligence normalizes dodge scores, cross-company contagion tracks language shifts across sectors, and BERTopic monitors emerging themes. A RAG-augmented agent answers complex queries step by step, citing transcripts and structured data. This week, the system stops treating companies as isolated data points and starts modeling the relationships between them.

props.sparkLine: This week: it stops reading them alone.

beats.narration_text: A company's signals don't exist in isolation. A Graph Attention Network now models the entire twenty-five-ticker universe as a network — companies as nodes, relationships as edges. Contagion links, supply chain connections, and sector membership all become edges with learnable weights. The model learns which connections carry predictive information and which don't. A company surrounded by neighbors whose language is a different profile than one with identical signals surrounded by stable peers. Same numbers, different context — and the graph captures that context.

Three upgrades to how the system reads language. First, a language model fine-tuned on the full transcript corpus — it now understands how executives frame guidance, not just general English. Every downstream NLP task gets better embeddings. Second, entity linking — when a CEO mentions a competitor by name, the system connects that mention to the competitor's own node in the company graph. Cross-transcript references become structured data. Third, signal-aware summarization generates a three-to-five-paragraph summary of every call, highlighting the sentences that matter most. No more reading full transcripts for routine monitoring.

Management makes claims and backs them with evidence. Argument mining now extracts that structure — the claim, the supporting evidence, and the implicit reasoning connecting them. It rates argument strength based on evidence specificity. A claim backed by a concrete number scores higher than one supported by vague qualitative language. And it tracks this over time. When a company keeps making bold claims but the evidence behind them gets thinner each quarter, that pattern of weakening arguments is itself a signal — and the system now detects it.

props.sparkLine: Weigh the claim against the backing.

beats.narration_text: Not every signal moves at the same speed. Wavelet decomposition separates each signal into frequency bands. Low-frequency components capture multi-year structural trends — these feed the Temporal Fusion Transformer for long-horizon forecasting. Mid-frequency components capture annual or semi-annual cycles — these feed Prophet for seasonality detection. And high-frequency components capture sharp quarter-to-quarter spikes — unexpected disruptions that don't fit either pattern. Each frequency band goes to the model built to handle it. One signal, three time scales, three different insights.

Twenty-two phases in, the system sees companies as nodes in a network, not isolated rows in a table. Domain-tuned language models read corporate speech with native fluency. Entity linking connects mentions across transcripts to the company graph. Argument mining catches the gap between what management claims and what the evidence supports. And wavelet decomposition lets every signal speak at its natural frequency. The system now understands not just what a company says, but who it's connected to and how strong the case really is. Next week, we keep building.

Let's recap with Claude. Every addition this week says the same thing in a different vocabulary: nothing in a transcript means very much on its own. A graph attention network stops treating a company as a self-contained row — the same numbers read differently depending on whether its neighbours are holding steady or coming apart. A domain-tuned language model stops reading corporate speech as general English, so two sentences that mean the same thing in this industry finally sit next to each other. Entity linking turns a mention of a rival into a pointer at that rival's own node. Argument mining stops taking a claim at face value and weighs it against whatever was offered to support it. And wavelet decomposition stops reading one signal at a single speed. The title is the thesis.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Most scoring systems treat each record as though it were the only one in the file. Paste this into Claude with something you already score, and work through three things — what surrounds each record, whether your model speaks your field's dialect or only general English, and where you are taking a claim at face value.

show.event: ClaudeComposerAsk: greeting 'Your turn.'; prompt types itself

props.command: I score records one at a time, as though each were independent. Can you help me with three things: one, work out what SURROUNDS each record — its neighbours, its parent, its peers — and whether a model that could see those relationships would actually beat the one I have, or just cost more to train; two, tell me whether my text model really speaks my field's dialect or is general English wearing a domain label, and how I would check that rather than assume it; and three, find the places where I accept a claim at face value without scoring whatever was offered as evidence for it.
